items.title: When AI Shows Its Rationale: User-Visible Rationale Styles and the Adoption of AI-Mediated Relational Correction
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support interpersonal communication, yet little is known about how user-visible rationales shape users’ evaluations of AI-assisted messages. We examine this question in Chinese family group chats, where correcting older relatives’ health misinformation requires factual accuracy alongside care, respect, and face management. In a between-subjects experiment (N = 279), participants viewed the same corrective reply preceded by no visible rationale, a procedural rationale, or a relational rationale. Both rationale conditions increased performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and adoption intention while reducing AI-mediated authenticity concern. Relational rationale produced the largest reduction in authenticity concern, and its effect on performance expectancy strengthened as affective load increased. Overall, user-visible rationales appear to function as communicative frames that shape how users evaluate AI-assisted interpersonal messages, extending research on explainable AI and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: Willingness to Use Personal Health Record Systems: A Mixed-Methods Study Among Multi-Ethnic Civil Servants in an Upper-Middle-Income Country
items.abstract: Background Electronic personal health record (PHR) systems allow individuals to access and manage their medical records seamlessly across healthcare providers to enhance service delivery and health outcomes. The success of the PHR systems depends on people’s willingness to use (WTU) them. Despite the increasing implementation of this technology in Malaysia, there is a lack of official documentation regarding its acceptance or adoption. Given its high implementation costs, it is essential to gauge the public’s WTU, assess the findings, and take appropriate measures to improve it. Methods This study aimed to determine the WTU as well as understand its predictors and insights among multi-ethnic civil servants from 15 ministries in Putrajaya, Malaysia, using a convergent mixed-methods study. The cross-sectional study was based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology with linear regression analysis. Meanwhile, the generic qualitative study was based on semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis. Results The majority of respondents were willing to use the PHR system both currently and in the future. Significant predictors of performance expectancy (PE), facilitating conditions (FC), and social influence (SI) were integrated with the six themes of PE, FC, SI, effort expectancy (EE), human factors (HF), and perceived risk (PR). PE influenced WTU through health status, convenience, administrative efficiency, and incentives, while FC encompassed accessibility, self-efficacy, and assistance. SI depended on the impact of the healthcare provider, social connections, social media figure, promotion, stranger, and sense of autonomy. As for EE, informants underscored the importance of system integration, stability, and user interface. Additionally, HF extended beyond age, gender, and experience to include race, education, income, and employment. Meanwhile, PR was in regard to security, privacy, information credibility, and legal instruments. Conclusion Addressing these domains through tailored strategies can fulfil population needs, enhance system optimization, increase user acceptance, and support sustainable nationwide PHR system adoption.

items.title: 4C/ID Training at UISRAEL
items.abstract: This repository provides materials from a professional development programme at Universidad Tecnológica Israel, Ecuador, on designing instruction around authentic professional tasks using the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C/ID) model. The programme helps university teachers connect syllabus learning outcomes with the integrated knowledge, skills and attitudes required for professional performance. The materials combine explanatory guides, worked design examples, classroom modelling, participant assignments and design worksheets. A continuing example (i.e., conducting a critical literature review to substantiate the preliminary definition of an educational research problem) illustrates how the design decisions connect across sessions. Participants apply the same principles to tasks from their own disciplines. The materials are shared to document the training and support scholarly discussion, reuse and adaptation in higher education. They describe the programme’s instructional rationale and activities; they do not report an empirical evaluation of its effectiveness.

items.title: Acceptance of Training Across Society of Automotive Engineers Levels of Driving Automation
items.abstract: As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become integrated into everyday transportation, developing accurate mental models of automated systems is essential for safe and effective human–vehicle interaction. Inspired by using pre-flight briefings in the aviation industry, this study examined participants’ perceptions of training across the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) levels of driving automation. Fifty-one U.S.-based participants were surveyed about their understandings of AV systems, their reliance behaviors on them, and preferences for training across five SAE levels. Our data revealed that most participants preferred receiving some form of training across all levels of automation. Individuals’ personal preferences for mandatory training increased with higher levels of automation and were strongly aligned with their beliefs on legally required training. Additionally, accessible onboarding approaches, particularly in-vehicle tutorials, were identified as the most preferred training format. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of supporting mental model formation to facilitate safe and effective use of AVs.

items.title: Are Workplace Tolerance and Individual Autonomy associated with Work Engagement? —Mediation analyses with Psychological Safety and Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

items.title: Between financial, digital, and graph literacy and fraud victimization: Disentangling components and cognitive biases
items.abstract: The rapid digitalisation of financial services has increased individuals’ exposure to online fraud. However, recent literature highlights that identifying a clear profile of fraud victims remains challenging, as individual-level factors examined so far do not fully explain fraud vulnerability. This study examines how financial literacy, digital financial literacy, and financial graph literacy are associated with individuals’ susceptibility to fraud. Moving beyond aggregate measures, the study adopts a multidimensional framework that distinguishes, for both financial and digital financial literacy, between knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, and introduces financial graph literacy as a key capability for interpreting visually presented financial information. The study combines survey-based measures with an embedded experimental task and employs regression and mediation analyses. The findings show that financial and digital financial knowledge are not consistently associated with lower fraud victimization. Higher financial and digital financial attitude scores are associated with lower fraud victimization, whereas higher scores on the financial behavior index are associated with greater reported victimization. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower fraud victimization. Indirect-effect estimates are consistent with partial mediation through overconfidence for digital financial attitude and financial graph literacy. Financial graph literacy is also associated with lower end-anchoring, i.e. a disproportionate reliance on the final movement of a stock-price graph, but end-anchoring is not associated with fraud victimization. Overall, the study advances a process-oriented and behaviorally grounded understanding of fraud vulnerability, emphasizing the interplay among literacy components and cognitive biases.

items.title: Biased Error Attribution in Multi-Agent Human–AI Systems Under Delayed Feedback
items.abstract: Human decision-making is often influenced by cognitive biases, especially under uncertainty and risk. Prior works have studied biases in single-step decision environments with immediate outcomes or in interaction with a single AI agent. However, less attention has been given to (1) cascaded settings with delayed outcomes, where decision at one step influences future system states and (2) to interaction with multiple AI agents. To study this, we designed a naval battle strategy game where participants interact with two AI advisors. We find asymmetric responses to positive and negative outcomes, with significant changes after negative outcomes. Participants failed to identify the actions responsible for failures and misattributed responsibility across AI agents, leading them to modify decisions steps weakly related to the true cause of poor performance. We refer to this behavior as bias in error attribution. Our findings show how cognitive biases can emerge in human-multi AI teams in cascaded settings.

items.title: Career choice motivations, perceptions, and future intentions among Indian nursing students: a mixed-methods study
items.abstract: Background: Ensuring a sustainable nursing workforce requires both academic capacity building and a deeper understanding of the experiences that nurture students’ commitment to the profession. In India, rapid growth in nursing education has intersected with changing societal perceptions and competitive career landscapes. This study sought to explore career choice motivations, professional perceptions, and future career intentions among Indian nursing students. Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods approach was gently conducted between April 2025 and June 2026. Phase I involved an online cross-sectional survey (N=1544) across multiple geographical zones. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Group comparison tests, and multiple linear regression modelling were also used. Phase II comprised semi-structured qualitative interviews (N=27) analyzed using Colaizzi’s descriptive phenomenological approach to better contextualize the statistical findings. Quantitative and qualitative strands were integrated via joint display and narrative synthesis. Results: A notable proportion of participants (69.8%) reported considering alternative career choices, most commonly medicine (37.4%) and technical fields (25.8%). Mean domain scores indicated high intrinsic motivation (19.94 ± 4.61) and economic expectations (20.00 ± 4.11), alongside academic stress (20.03 ± 3.90). Multiple regression analysis (F = 5.085, p < 0.001, R² = 0.103) showed that female gender (B = 4.717, p < 0.001) and salary expectations (B = 1.493, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perception scores, whereas career change intention (B = −4.659, p < 0.001) and higher secondary examination marks (B = −1.905, p = 0.002) were negatively associated. Qualitative findings, organized into seven themes and 27 subthemes, provided explanatory context. Students described how entrance exam setbacks, heavy assignment loads, inconsistent mentorship, and social stigma contributed to uncertainty. In contrast, rewarding patient encounters and the development of clinical confidence fostered a growing sense of professional commitment. Conclusion: Indian nursing students navigate diverse pathways into the profession, balancing altruistic goals with practical challenges and evolving career preferences. The results tentatively highlight that supportive career counseling, refined academic requirements, enhanced clinical mentorship, and clear role definitions may help strengthen students' professional identity and support long-term commitment to nursing practice.

items.title: Children’s Engagement during Cognitive Assessments with Minimal Robot Intervention
items.abstract: Standard pediatric cognitive and projective assessments can be monotonous and provoke anxiety. This reduces children's engagement and compliance and diminishes the quality of observable behavior. In this work, we present a workflow that transfers routine paper-and-pencil tasks to a tablet application and adds a NAO humanoid robot as a social partner. Our goal is to provide a robot-and-tablet system for standardized assessments. In this exploratory study, we focused on quantifying the added contribution of the robot to engagement compared to a tablet-only system. To this end, we evaluated the workflow in a pediatric clinic with 24 participants, each with a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosis, using a controlled, between-subjects design. The tablet-only condition delivered the same activities and pacing without robot cues. This served as a control to isolate the effect of social scaffolding. Licensed therapists rated engagement using the Pediatric Assessment of Rehabilitation Engagement (PARE) scale. Our preliminary findings suggest that the robot's presence supported higher observable engagement and sustained participation without altering the rapport within the child–therapist–robot triad. Moreover, results in the PARE scale were significantly different between the two conditions when considering the age of the little patients (with mean age 10 vs. 8, respectively). While the small sample size and age distribution warrant cautious interpretation, this work highlights a robot's potential contribution to children's engagement during standardized assessment.

items.title: Cognitive Friction in Human-AI Interactions Across Learning, Work, and Everyday Use: A Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Cognitive friction has been described both as productive resistance intended to sustain cognitive engagement and as effort required to overcome obstacles in AI interaction. These uses create uncertainty about the boundaries of the construct and the mechanisms attributed to it across different contexts. To clarify how cognitive friction is defined and distinguished from related constructs, and to map the mechanisms described as generating it across educational, professional, and everyday human–AI interactions. English-language empirical and non-empirical sources will be eligible where they provide substantive conceptual or mechanistic content relevant to cognitive friction or potentially related constructs in human–AI interaction. Eligible evidence may include journal articles, conference papers, theses, substantive commentaries, and full preprints or working papers. Electronic searches were conducted on 22 October 2026 in Scopus, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, arXiv and SSRN. Backward and forward citation searching will supplement these searches. Two reviewers will independently screen records and assess full texts against predefined eligibility criteria. Two reviewers will independently chart data using a structured Google Sheets workbook. Data will be analysed through descriptive mapping and basic qualitative content analysis. No formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment will be conducted.

items.title: Converged Security Maturity Index: A Unified Model for Cyber, Physical, and Operational Security Maturity Assessment
items.abstract: The growing integration of cyber, physical, and operational security functions has created a need for assessment approaches that evaluate security convergence as an organisational capability rather than as a set of isolated controls. This article proposes the Converged Security Maturity Index (CSMI), a conceptual maturity model designed to assess the level of integration among cybersecurity, physical security, and operational security within organisations. The model is developed using a design science research approach grounded in a structured review of converged security literature, cyber–physical system security, and existing maturity frameworks. CSMI comprises five progressive maturity levels—Fragmented, Coordinated, Integrated, Unified, and Optimised—and evaluates organisational capabilities across four dimensions: governance and strategy, processes and incident management, technology and infrastructure integration, and human factors and organisational culture. The article describes the architecture of the model and the rationale for each maturity level and dimension and outlines how the framework could be applied in practice through a structured questionnaire in future work. The proposed framework aims to support organisational self-assessment, benchmarking, and identification of convergence gaps across different sectors.

items.title: Do Default Effects Shape Cyber Attack Decisions? Lessons From an Empirical Study
items.abstract: Understanding cognitive biases in cyber attacker behavior can help develop countermeasures that leverage predictable mental shortcuts. This paper analyzes the impact of one such bias, the default effect, on cyber attack decisions. Three forms of this effect are examined: explicit default, association effect, and position effect. The experiment included 85 participants who displayed cybersecurity knowledge based on a screening assessment. The participants performed established behavioral tasks and cyber-adapted scenarios involving host selection, port selection, and password spraying. Our findings confirmed that explicit defaults behave as expected from prior research: people preferred the default option more often under opt-out than opt-in framing. For cyber tasks, the association effect was always present and influential as participants preferred options semantically related to the contextual cues provided. In contrast, position effects failed to emerge when semantically meaningful cues were available. Results offer actionable insights for designing cyber defense systems that leverage predictable attacker heuristics.

items.title: Exploring the usage of transparency in supervising uncrewed air traffic management systems
items.abstract: To safely and efficiently manage increasing drone traffic, Uncrewed Air Traffic Management (UTM) is currently being developed with high levels of automation. In low-altitude airspace around airports, human supervision remains essential to ensure safe separation between drones and crewed aircraft, requiring transparency to support oversight of automated decision-making. Although transparency has been shown to improve understanding, trust, and performance, relatively little is known about transparency-seeking behavior during real-time supervision. This article presents a novel on-demand interface for tactical UTM, comprising eight information overlays derived from a consolidated transparency taxonomy that unifies previously fragmented transparency constructs. A human-in-the-loop experiment with 16 participants investigated transparency usage under varying traffic conditions, automation failures, and two autonomous path-planning algorithms: the graph-based Zeta*-SIPP and the sampling-based Informed RRT*. The results show that information about the Closest Point of Approach between drones and crewed aircraft was operationally most valuable. During automation failures, participants increasingly requested information about changes in constraints and traffic situations, together with the planner’s internal reasoning, to diagnose failures and guide intervention decisions. Furthermore, the sampling-based planner revealed an important boundary condition for transparency research: the cognitive costs and benefits of algorithmic transparency during real-time supervision depend on the characteristics of the underlying algorithm and how its search process is presented. Overall, this study shows that transparency requirements are dynamic, depending on user needs, operational context, and the underlying autonomy, and that complementary transparency perspectives can be successfully integrated into a single adaptable interface.

items.title: FRAM-FDM: A Quantitative Safety-II Framework for Runway Overrun Risk Assessment Using Functional Resonance Analysis and Flight Data Monitoring
items.abstract: Runway overruns rank among the most frequent and economically significant accident categories in commercial aviation, typically arising from the nonlinear combination of performance variabilities during the approach and landing phases. Existing risk models either rely on historical accident databases or treat runway overrun precursors as independent binary events, overlooking the interactive dynamics of everyday flight operations. This paper introduces FRAM-FDM, a quantitative methodology that integrates the Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM) with Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) to assess and manage operational runway overrun risk from a Safety-II perspective. The methodology deconstructs the approach-and-landing sociotechnical system into functional couplings, quantifies their output variabilities using real flight data recorder (FDR) data, and aggregates them through: (i) linear regression combined with Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) for probabilistic fleet-level risk estimation; (ii) logistic regression with odds-ratio analysis to rank precursor influence; and (iii) metadata-driven scenario simulation in the FRAM Model Visualiser (FMV). Applied to a case study of 110 landings — including one overrun event — from a business jet fleet, the framework identifies airspeed excess at the runway threshold and brake application profile as the dominant risk contributors, demonstrates synergistic risk amplification when multiple variabilities co-occur, and provides actionable guidance for training and procedure reinforcement. FRAM-FDM advances FRAM toward a fully quantitative, data-driven implementation and aligns FDM programmes with Safety-II principles.

items.title: Frequency and purpose of artificial intelligence tool use and their associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy among medical students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used by medical students for academic purposes, yet how patterns of such use relate to academic motivation and self-efficacy remain insufficiently characterized, particularly in the Iranian medical education context. This study examined the frequency and purpose of AI tool use among medical students and their associations with academic motivation and academic self-efficacy. Methods A descriptive-analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among medical students at Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Iran, in 2026. Using proportionate stratified sampling across four educational stages, 111 students completed a questionnaire package comprising a researcher-developed AI-use instrument (separate frequency and purpose scores), the Persian Academic Motivation Scale, and the Persian College Academic Self-Efficacy Scale. Associations between the two AI-use scores and five outcomes (self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, amotivation, and composite positive motivation) were examined using Spearman correlation with Bonferroni correction, followed by five multiple linear regression models adjusting for age, sex, educational stage, and GPA. Results Conversational AI tools, most notably ChatGPT, were used by nearly all participants. Both AI-use frequency and purpose were positively correlated with academic self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, and negatively correlated with amotivation (Spearman ρ = 0.46–0.77; all p < 0.001, surviving Bonferroni correction). In adjusted models, AI-use purpose remained independently associated with all five outcomes (standardized β = 0.32–0.69), whereas AI-use frequency remained independently associated only with self-efficacy (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). GPA was independently associated with intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, and positive motivation, but not self-efficacy or amotivation. No significant differences by sex or educational stage were observed. The five models explained 40% to 61% of outcome variance. Conclusions The purpose for which medical students use AI tools showed more consistent independent associations with academic motivation and self-efficacy than frequency of use alone, suggesting that how AI is used may be more relevant to these outcomes than how often it is used. As an observational, cross-sectional study, these findings describe association rather than causal sequence, and contribute context-specific evidence on AI use and its psychological correlates among medical students in Iran.

items.title: How communicating an AI’s relational risk influences trust perceptions in AI-assisted decision-making
items.abstract: AI systems err, however, existing Strategies to influence a user’s trust perception can sometimes fail to foster perceptions and assessments that reflect system limitations, with potentially detrimental real-world consequences. In this paper, we introduce a novel Relational Risk (RR) strategy derived from risk communication research to pre-emptively communicate the likelihood of AI error and its potential consequences, foregrounding the costs of AI error, and compare it with existing Strategies (AI accuracy, AI apology). Participants ( ) engaged in an AI-assisted decision-making task with varying Stakes and AI performance, and we measured how these influence perceived AI trustworthiness across relevant perceptual dimensions (transparency, performance, utility). We find that RR enhances perceived AI transparency post-AI errors and encourages healthy scrutiny without diminishing or inflating perceived AI performance or utility. Conversely, AI accuracy boosts perceived AI transparency, performance, and utility under high decision-stakes, increasing system trustworthiness when unwarranted, while apology improves perceived AI utility but does not support system understanding. We contribute an in-depth investigation of how communication strategies shape AI trustworthiness perceptions, reveal important drawbacks of existing approaches, and demonstrate how integrating risk communication theory can enable more appropriate trustworthiness assessments.

items.title: How much can a human being lift? A Bayesian latent capability model for Olympic weightlifting
items.abstract: Estimates of the limits of human performance are usually built on record books, on the premise that a record is the best an athlete could do. In Olympic weightlifting the premise fails, because the competitor declares the weight before each of three attempts per lift and only the heaviest successful attempt is recorded, so a record is a lower bound, chosen by the athlete, on a maximal capability never observed. We treat the maximal lift of each competitor on each competition day as a latent variable, of which every attempt is a trial and every declared weight a measurement. Its distribution at a given bodyweight follows an extreme value mixture model with an estimated threshold, and an athlete-specific random effect links the competitions of each athlete. The model is fitted to the 117,892 attempts of 5,040 athletes in 141 international competitions between 2017 and 2026. The upper tail of capability is bounded, with posterior probability above 0.999 for men, 0.96 for the women's snatch and 0.94 for the women's clean and jerk. At 110 kilograms of bodyweight the men's ceiling lies one to three per cent above the heaviest lifts, against twelve and sixteen per cent for women at 86 kilograms. The record book alone places the men's ceiling six and twelve kilograms higher, because the best lift of a day ending on a success overstates capability.

items.title: Minimally Invasive Surgery and Emerging Technologies in Emergency Abdominal Surgery: A Narrative Review Focusing on Indocyanine Green Fluorescence, Robotic Assistance and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is progressively transforming emergency abdominal care through high-definition visualization, indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging, robotic-assisted platforms and the emerging integration of artificial intelligence (AI). This narrative review traces the evolution from conventional laparoscopy to fluorescence-guided, robotic-assisted and AI-supported emergency surgery. Publications were identified in PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science, prioritizing guidelines, consensus statements, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and recent clinical studies. Current evidence supports a laparoscopic-first approach in hemodynamically stable patients with acute appendicitis, acute calculous cholecystitis, perforated peptic ulcer and selected cases of adhesive small bowel obstruction, strangulated hernia, complicated diverticulitis and penetrating trauma, whereas open laparotomy remains mandatory in hemorrhagic or septic shock. Near-infrared ICG imaging has expanded from elective to emergency practice for biliary anatomy identification, bowel perfusion assessment and anastomotic decision-making, although prospective emergency data remain limited. Robotic systems offer dexterity, ergonomics and integrated imaging, but emergency use is constrained by availability, cost, docking time and team training. AI is being explored for anatomy recognition, risk prediction, augmented reality and autonomous subtasks, with decision support the most realistic near-term role. The value of these technologies depends less on the technology itself than on patient selection, surgical expertise, team preparedness and institutional readiness.

items.title: Online, offline, and hybrid identity: Exploring domain-based social identities and their implications for technology attitudes, wellbeing, and social cohesion
items.abstract: Online identity typically has been conceptualized either in terms of online social roles or in terms of identification with specific online groups. In this paper we explore whether people can form a meaningful identity from the online domain itself , seeing themselves collectively as ‘online people’, ‘offline people’, or in terms of a hybrid online/offline self-categorization. Results from a survey study of 200 participants supported this idea, such that the means of online, offline, or hybrid person variables were significantly above the midpoint of the scale and the majority of participants identified most strongly in terms of one of these identities. Factor analysis, correlations, variable network analysis, and textual analysis suggested that online and offline social identity are orthogonal constructs. Moreover, online identity was related to, but distinct from, hybrid identity (being a person who lives both online and offline). Supporting predictions derived from social digital identity theory (SDIT), each kind of domain-based identification uniquely predicted higher trust in the relevant ingroup only. Moreover, in line with predictions, online identification uniquely predicted more positive attitudes towards technology. However, contrary to predictions, the different kinds of domain-based social identification did not uniquely predict wellbeing or social cohesion. Hybrid and offline identification also failed to uniquely predict technology attitudes. Furthermore, when controlling for hybrid identification, being more ‘online’ in terms of online technology use did not significantly predict wellbeing or social cohesion outcomes. These findings represent an initial exploration of ‘domain-based’ social identities and their implications.

items.title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
items.abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

items.title: Repertoires of Contention: Building computational tools and infrastructures for community resistance to bitcoin mining
items.abstract: Recent work in human-computer interaction and allied fields has sought to engage community members as co-designers, facilitators, and decision makers to challenge structural power barriers and knowledge gaps. In this paper, we apply a diverse set of computational techniques to engage and address community concerns surrounding the socio-environmental impacts of the Greenidge Bitcoin mining power plant facility in upstate New York. Through collaborative interactions with community groups, addressing problems ranging from regulatory inertia to thermal water pollution, we aim to facilitate not just the production of new and critical environmental knowledge but also new computationally-supported repertoires of contention: means of contesting the unequal relations of knowledge and power that structure and often determine the outcomes of environmental controversies. We argue such engagements can help support more politically engaged forms of HCI, oriented towards efforts to redress and repair disparities in wealth, knowledge, and influence through strategic sociotechnical interventions and alliances.

items.title: To Bot or not To Bot: Integrating a Social Robot into the Actor’s Rehearsal Process
items.abstract: Effective theatrical rehearsal is essential for actors’ character development, involving intricate cognitive, emotional, and physical processes. Despite well-established traditional techniques that combine individual practice and partner interactions, rehearsal often requires significant time and resources. Emerging digital and robotic technologies present novel opportunities to enhance rehearsal methods; however, their potential as interactive rehearsal aids remains largely unexplored. This research examines the role of a social robot in supporting actors during pre-rehearsal or solo preparation of two scenes from Tennessee Williams’ The Glass Menagerie (1944). Thirty actors with different levels of experience participated in three rehearsal settings: solo practice, rehearsal with a robot playing one character, and rehearsal with the robot alternating between two roles. We evaluated the robot's impact via qualitative responses and self-reports. Thematic analysis indicated that robot-assisted rehearsal improved participants’ experience compared to solo rehearsal, especially among less experienced actors. The robot's role-switching capability offered additional depth appreciated mainly by seasoned performers. These outcomes highlight the promise of social robots as rehearsal tools adapted to the experience of actors.

items.title: Understanding organisations’ responsibilities and readiness for occupational road safety: Implications for saving lives beyond 2025
items.abstract: Most organisations generate travel and transport and thus influence traffic safety. Nevertheless, their roles and responsibilities for occupational road safety remain poorly understood. This study examines organisational readiness for occupational road safety with a particular focus on the relationship between organisations’ perceptions of traffic safety and the implementation of traffic safety measures. The study is based on a survey of organisational representatives in 109 companies in Sweden in 2025. The survey consists of two questionnaires capturing organisational commitment and reported measures to improve traffic safety in organisations’ roles as employers and transport buyers. An employer questionnaire focuses on traffic safety requirements for employees’ work-related travel and organisational vehicle fleets, while a transport procurement questionnaire captures the requirements on transport procurement. Organisational readiness for occupational road safety is analysed using Organisational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC), including perceived capacity to influence traffic safety, views on responsibility, and the integration of traffic safety into occupational health and safety (OHS) or sustainability practices. The results show that many organisations have policies for work-related travel and set traffic safety requirements for their vehicles, while such requirements in transport procurement remain limited. Regression analyses indicate that organisations with higher readiness are more likely to set traffic safety requirements, particularly regarding work-related travel. The findings highlight the need to strengthen organisations’ awareness of their roles and responsibilities, clarify expectations for organisations from authorities, and further integrate traffic safety into organisational management systems to reduce road traffic fatalities and injuries, in line with the global road safety agenda, often framed as “saving lives beyond 2025”.

items.title: What makes human contribution recognisable in AI-mediated work? Attributional labour and gendered recognition in apprenticeships in England
items.abstract: Debates around generative artificial intelligence frequently organise workplace change through automation and augmentation, leaving less visible the organisational work through which human contribution remains interpretable once production is shared with generative systems. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 women in business-related apprenticeships in England, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and abductive engagement with sociotechnical AI research, labour-process scholarship and feminist accounts of recognition, the study develops a mechanism-oriented account in which organisational rules delimit legitimate AI use, selected execution tasks accelerate, and verification, contextual judgement and accountable decision-making remain attached to apprentices. Where AI-mediated production made polished output a weaker standalone indicator of individual capability, some participants described supplementing performance with additional evidentiary work that rendered contribution, judgement and responsibility more legible to evaluators. This evaluator-facing work is conceptualised as attributional labour, a reconfiguration of pre-existing recognition demands whose form changes when technologically mediated artefacts reveal less about the human competence behind them. The organisational costs and returns associated with this work appeared to vary with occupational hierarchy, managerial proximity and the valuation of administrative and relational work. Augmentation consequently emerges as an organisational recognition settlement in which technical capacity, hidden human work and evaluative authority are redistributed together.

items.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

items.title: Climate heat disasters fuel the health and care workforce crisis: a comparative assessment of workforce heat-health policy in selected European countries
items.abstract: Background. A majority of European countries have heat-health action plans in place or under development, yet the health and social sectors are poorly considered despite their high burden and key role for health system resilience and security. Objectives. This research connects workforce policy and heat-health action policy, aiming to assess preparedness, protection and agency of health and care workers and identify gaps and capacities for implementation. Methods. Qualitative comparative methodology and a country case study design were applied and a rapid assessment of eight European countries performed during August/September 2026. A semi-structed topic guide informed data collection, drawing on policy documents and other secondary sources. Results. No country case study established a dedicated workforce-centred heat-health strategy nor do they have routine workforce-specific heat-health surveillance systems in place. Countries recognise health workers primarily as service providers, rather than as a workforce requiring protection. This approach shapes all areas of heat-health action. Preparedness of health workers shows limited strategic action but with some adaptations at the provider and individual level and in the education sector. Protection remains poorly addressed and equality, gender equality and migrant health workers are largely absent. Professional stakeholders and bottom-up emerging adaptations create capacities but agency is limited. Four interrelated priorities for advancing workforce heat-health policy can be identified: alignment of heat-health policy and occupational health law; workforce-specific surveillance and monitoring; stakeholder involvement and transsectoral governance; and a European Union strategy. Conclusions. Workforce resilience and climate-health resilience must be addressed together to ensure health security.

items.title: CoT4AD: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Explicit Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently attracted growing attention in end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving. While recent works have begun exploring Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to decompose complex driving tasks, they predominantly rely on purely textual reasoning. Driving, however, is an inherently spatial and physical task. Textual-only CoT struggles to capture dynamic geometric changes, frequently leading to numerical hallucinations and unreliable trajectory planning. To bridge the gap between semantic reasoning and the physical action space, we propose CoT4AD, a novel VLA framework that introduces a Hybrid Visual-Language CoT. Grounded in human cognitive Situation Awareness (SA) theory, CoT4AD strictly enforces a causal reasoning sequence: 3D spatial perception, semantic comprehension via Visual Question Answering (VQA), and physical projection via VLM-conditioned future scene diffusion. This hybrid chain explicitly forces the VLM to respect physical laws and spatial constraints before outputting driving trajectories. Furthermore, to balance explicit interpretability with the stringent latency demands of real-world deployment, we introduce an Implicit CoT model via Latent Alignment. This approach distills the multi-step causal knowledge directly into the VLM's hidden states, enabling highly efficient inference without sacrificing reasoning capability. Extensive experiments on both real-world and simulated benchmarks demonstrate that CoT4AD achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, it reaches a leading Driving Score of 81.22 on the Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark and significantly reduces collision rates in nuScenes open-loop evaluations, proving the necessity and effectiveness of physics-grounded visual reasoning in E2E autonomous driving.

items.title: Counteracting threat bias: A longitudinal field experiment testing two interventions that expand managerial attention to opportunities under economic threat.
items.abstract: When economic threat is salient, managers focus on preventing losses and neglect the opportunities adaptation requires, a pattern termed threat bias. On the prevailing view, managerial attention is limited so that attention to threat comes at the expense of attention to opportunity: Restoring it means perceiving less threat or relaxing vigilance, and the remedy has been to divide the orientations across people or units. Drawing on regulatory focus theory, in which promotion and prevention are independent systems, I propose instead that threat bias reflects a situational construal: Salient threat makes prevention cues dominant, while promotion cues lie dormant, so their relation is not fixed. I test this with two brief construal-shaping interventions, one highlighting opportunities (opportunity) and one highlighting opportunities and threats (balanced), in a five-wave field experiment with 414 managers during the COVID-19 downturn, with voice rated by higher level managers blind to condition. Among unexposed managers, within-person increases in perceived threat were associated with lower promotion focus and opportunity-related voice, the threat-bias pattern. Both interventions weakened that association and raised promotion focus and opportunity-related voice relative to control, under sustained economic threat. The balanced intervention also increased prevention focus and threat-related voice; the opportunity intervention changed neither. Mean perceived threat was unchanged: The interventions altered how managers responded to threat, not how much threat they perceived. Intervention effects on voice grew over 3 months. Threat bias therefore reflects how managers construe the situation rather than an unavoidable trade-off between the orientations, and both can be raised in the same managers at once. items.title: Different Logics, Similar Intentions: Heterogeneity in How Employees Evaluate AI Adoption
items.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption at work has documented heterogeneity in user attitudes and adoption profiles, but less is known about whether employees differ in how they weight adoption-relevant information. In a within-subject structured-profile experiment, 446 employees provided 7,136 intention judgments across 16 profiles that varied AI adoption benefits, barriers, replacement vulnerability, and anticipated work harm. Multilevel regression mixture model analysis identified four latent decision-policy classes with different estimated weights on opportunity and threat cues; class mean intentions were not statistically distinguishable. Drawing on multiple-cue judgment theory, we interpret this pattern as heterogeneity in cue utilization rather than simply in attitude levels. Explaining and managing AI adoption therefore requires attention to latent decision policies, because aggregate effect estimates and profiles based on mean levels can conceal differences in cue responsiveness that shape how employees evaluate AI.

items.title: Evaluating AI Alignment in LLMs: Output Analysis of Value Priorities Across 75 Models with Human Benchmarking
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) shape human–AI interaction, yet capability and safety benchmarks provide limited insight into their expressed value priorities. Across three studies, we developed an output-based approach to evaluating correspondence between LLM priorities and human judgements of optimal AI functioning. Study 1 identified six themes through inductive qualitative analysis: Performance, Adaptive Capacity, Social Good, Ethics and Responsibility, Relational Integration, and Agency. Study 2 found stable rankings within models and a shared priority structure across models. Study 3 compared 75 LLMs with 376 human respondents using a profile-fidelity metric combining profile shape and calibration of between-priority differences. Many models reproduced the human profile while exaggerating differences between priorities. Fidelity varied across models, with no clear pattern linking fidelity to more recent releases. Both humans and LLMs assigned Agency low priority. This framework offers a standardized method for auditing expressed value profiles across models alongside capability, safety, and output evaluations.

items.title: Feeling Easier, Working Harder: Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Comprehension
items.abstract: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

items.title: From Briefing to Prompt: How Users Translate Textual Design Instructions into Text-to-Image Prompts
items.abstract: Text-to-image systems support creative, educational, and professional work, yet how users translate briefs into effective prompts remains underexplored. This study examines prompt formulation and refinement by 23 participants using ChatGPT with DALL·E 3 under two task configurations: low-detail briefings with multiple reformulations and high-detail briefings with one reformulation. A structured literature review and qualitative analysis of 81 prompts, 81 images, interviews, and observation notes, supported by inter-coder agreement, identified recurring strategies, difficulties expressing visual intentions, and refinement patterns. High-detail/single-reformulation tasks produced semantically denser prompts and closer alignment with intended outcomes; low-detail/multiple-reformulation tasks encouraged exploratory prompting and interpretive variation. Because briefing detail and reformulation opportunities varied together, these findings reflect task-configuration differences, not isolated effects of briefing complexity. Framing prompting as cognitive and creative mediation in human–AI interaction, the study proposes a process model spanning briefing interpretation, semantic extraction, visual attribute selection, prompt structuring, generation, and refinement, requiring further validation.

items.title: From driving (L0) to living (L5): Intergenerational car comfort concept by Etic-emic theory
items.abstract: This study explores intergenerational vehicle comfort using the Etic-Emic framework, translating a psychological concept into automotive guidelines. A scoping review identified 34 parameters, and trend analysis of 1789 Scopus articles (1953-2025) tracing comfort across vehicle generations. Expert interviews with 15 specialists classified them as Etic (relevant to L0 and L5) or Emic (emerging specifically in L5), suggesting additional factors. Group brainstorming refined classifications, yielding 44 parameters, including factors such as brand identity and cargo space. Safety, vibration control, and fuel efficiency were stable Etic parameters, whereas non-driving tasks, confidence to sleep or fully recline, legal liability transparency, and cybersecurity were Emic. The novel "Intergenerational Car Comfort" concept provides OEMs an actionable decision tool: its Etic-Emic matrix guides trade-offs, including safety constraints versus expectations to recline and sleep. Ultimately, it identifies legacy architectures to retain or those requiring new interior packaging and HMI solutions, providing a roadmap for next-generation automated vehicles.

items.title: From isolated countermeasures to organizational practice: A systematic review of workplace fatigue-management strategies in healthcare
items.abstract: Occupational fatigue poses persistent workforce and safety risks in healthcare. Other safety–critical sectors manage fatigue through structured fatigue risk management systems (FRMS), but whether healthcare’s evidence supports similar system-level claims is unclear. This systematic review synthesized evidence on the effects, implementation, and certainty of workplace fatigue-management strategies in healthcare. PubMed, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched through 1 June 2026. Studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, synthesized narratively per Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guidance, and assessed for implementation and certainty using Proctor’s framework and GRADE. Thirty-four publications representing 32 studies were included across four strategy groups: work-schedule and duty-hour controls; multicomponent programs and education/coaching; nap and restorative-break practices; and digital monitoring and real-time countermeasures. No included study evaluated a complete, formally governed fatigue risk management system; the evidence concerned isolated or bundled workplace strategies. Naps and restorative breaks showed the most recurrent short-term signals for reduced fatigue/sleepiness and improved vigilance or cognitive performance, though findings were inconsistent; evidence for other strategies was weaker, and patient-safety, organizational, and economic outcomes were rarely evaluated. Implementation evidence concentrated on acceptability and fidelity; organizational governance, structured risk assessment, reach, cost, and sustainability were unexamined, and certainty was predominantly low or very low, with one moderate-certainty exception for increased sleep duration under reduced-duty schedules. Healthcare has thus tested individual countermeasures rather than embedded fatigue risk management within organizational practice; advancing the field requires linking local hazards to supported controls, with particular attention to the governance and risk-assessment structures that remain least developed.

items.title: GeoST: Object-Local Representations and Geometric Support-Guided Temporal Fusion for Maritime Ship Detection in Point Clouds
items.abstract: Reliable environmental perception is essential for intelligent ships, with three-dimensional (3D) point cloud ship detection providing spatial information for situational awareness and collision avoidance. However, unstable cross-frame geometric correspondence, ambiguous historical associations, and unreliable temporal fusion hinder the use of historical information. We propose GeoST for temporal maritime LiDAR ship detection, using object-local representations as a basis for geometric support-guided historical feature modulation and fusion. Built on FASTer, GeoST normalizes observations within their respective proposal coordinate systems and associates them by object dimensions and shape, constructing temporal inputs without external ego-vessel poses. The multi-scale anisotropic point feature enhancement module (PointMKDA) aggregates neighborhood features across scales and orientations to enhance local geometric representations. The geometrically constrained cross-attention module (GCAM) uses enhanced current-frame focal point features to update historical features and estimate geometric support. The reliability-guided feature modulation (RGFM) module combines this support, association priors, observation age, and learned features to generate modulation weights across temporal, point, and channel dimensions, regulating feature contributions before temporal fusion. GeoST achieved 3D average precision (AP) of 87.17% and 73.09% at intersection-over-union (IoU) thresholds of 0.5 and 0.7, respectively, exceeding FASTer by 2.81 and 2.27 percentage points.

items.title: Not Interchangeable: Pilot Self-Reports and Instructor Competency Ratings as Cognitive-State Labels in Real Flight Operations
items.abstract: Objective To quantify the correspondence between pilots’ post-task workload and situation-awareness ratings and instructor competency ratings during real flight. Background Adaptive systems, neuroergonomic classifiers, and competency-based training all need cognitive-state labels. Self-reports capture felt demand and awareness; instructor evaluations capture behaviorally inferred competence. Method Forty pilots completed five Cessna 172 tasks during dedicated research flights. After each task, pilots gave single-item 0–10 ratings of workload and situation awareness. One flight instructor at each of the two participating organizations rated Situation Awareness and Workload Management on 1–4 International Civil Aviation Organization-aligned scales, and rated task execution with behavior-specific items, before hearing the self-ratings. Analyses used Spearman correlations with participant-clustered bootstrap intervals, within-person decomposition, and mixed-model and stratified sensitivity analyses. Results Pooled cross-source correspondence was weak for situation awareness ( ρ = . 08 ) and workload ( ρ = − . 14 ; . 14 aligned). The two instructor competencies were strongly intercorrelated ( ρ = . 61 ) and strongly associated with same-instructor task-execution ratings ( ρ = . 69 and . 72 ). A small within-person workload signal ( r = − . 19 ) attenuated after double centering. Point estimates were similar in both strata and after excluding pilots aged 60 or older. Conclusion The two sources provided distinct, non-substitutable labels. Their strong link to same-rater task-execution scores is consistent with execution-referenced judgment, though shared-rater variance cannot be ruled out; self-reports captured pilots’ reported experience. Application Cognitive-state monitoring and training assessment should use multi-source labels and should not treat observation-based competency ratings as direct measures of internal workload or situation awareness.

items.title: Occupational Health Risks: Personal Protective Equipment Utilisation and Exposures Among Healthcare Workers Ho West District, Ghana
items.abstract: Introduction: This study assessed occupational exposures, personal protective equipment (PPE) availability and utilisation, and factors associated with PPE utilisation among healthcare workers (HCWs) in Ho West District, Ghana. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 174 randomly selected HCWs from all 32 health facilities. Data collected using a structured, self-administered questionnaire in Kobo Collect were analysed in Stata 17. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests and logistic regression were used, with statistical significance set at p<0.05 and a 95% confidence level. Results: Overall, 79.3% of HCWs reported occupational exposure; 112 (64.4%) reported inadequate PPE availability, while 102 (58.6%) had poor PPE utilisation. Gloves were used by 75.3%, compared with gowns (5.8%) and eye protection (3.5%). Blood/body-fluid splashes were reported by 102 (58.6%) and needle-stick injuries by 73 (42.0%); 51.7% reported that exposures occurred rarely. PPE training was associated with higher odds of appropriate utilisation (AOR=2.75, 95% CI: 1.36–5.56; p=0.005), whereas economising on limited PPE supplies was associated with lower odds (AOR=0.34, 95% CI: 0.17–0.69; p=0.003). Conclusion: HCWs in Ho West District experienced substantial occupational exposure alongside inadequate PPE availability and generally poor utilisation. Regular practical training and a reliable, uninterrupted PPE supply are needed to improve appropriate use and reduce occupational risks.

items.title: Progressive Trajectory-Aware Calibration for Human–AI Handoff in Sales Conversations
items.abstract: AI assistants in sales conversations predict conversion probabilities at each turn, but miscalibrated confidence can undermine human–AI handoff decisions. We propose Progressive Trajectory-Aware Calibration (PTAC), a lightweight post-hoc method that adjusts temperature using conversation progress and observed probability trajectories. PTAC requires fewer than 5,000 parameters. On e-commerce data with independently verified outcomes, PTAC reduced turn-stratified calibration error by over 80% at 14% purchase prevalence and by 9% relative to static scaling at the natural 6% prevalence, matching adaptive scaling. It reduced error by 63–78% on call-center data with model-generated labels and by 13% on synthetic dialogues. PTAC improved handoff error rates at fixed human workloads and reduced misplaced reliance at operational thresholds; trust outcomes were simulated and matched-trust performance was comparable. Causal-progress ablation supported deployment-time improvements on call-center and synthetic data; e-commerce gains depended on non-causal turn position.

items.title: Social movements in the production of healthy, sustainable, and health-promoting territories: a scoping review
items.abstract: Health promotion and surveillance, encompassing environmental and occupational aspects, and grounded in a participatory, territory-based approach, integrate a set of concepts designed to support interventions addressing health issues experienced by populations within their own territories (Oliveira; Machado, 2026). The setting where surveillance and health promotion converge is almost invariably the territory, which serves as a central category for analyzing health-disease-care processes. This is because the territory extends beyond its geographical and material dimensions, incorporating social relations, identities, ways of life, cultural practices, and the processes involved in the production and reproduction of life (Santos, 2005). Understanding health-disease-care processes within a specific territory requires an interdependence between health surveillance, which seeks to identify risks, threats, and vulnerabilities affecting populations, and health promotion, which aims to intervene in the determinants that influence living conditions. These approaches encompass various fields of action, including epidemiology, public health, environmental health, and occupational health. Their combined efforts contribute to the prevention of health issues, the reduction of risks, and the development of responses tailored to the specific needs of these territories (Teixeira, 2002; Oliveira & Machado, 2026). The primary milestone in defining health promotion globally is the Ottawa Charter (WHO, 1986), developed at the First International Conference on Health Promotion, which posits an expanded concept of health, one encompassing quality of life. Health is linked to access to culture, leisure, sports, work, employment, income, education, housing, social assistance, and healthy environments, among various other dimensions that serve as determinants for the living and health conditions of populations, communities, and territories (Brazil, 2018). Furthermore, promoting health on a global scale has entailed developing intersectoral and participatory actions that enhance the autonomy of individuals and communities, strengthening their collective capacities and contributing to the transformation of the conditions that generate inequalities (Brazil, 2018). After all, no one falls ill or recovers alone; everyone falls ill and recovers collectively, within a community (Teixeira, 2002; Oliveira; Machado, 2026). This expanded conception highlights that health promotion cannot be understood as the exclusive responsibility of health services and professionals; rather, its realization depends on recognizing the diverse ways of being and existing in the world, constructed within specific territories and shaped by socio-environmental determinants (Breilh, 2006). For instance, communities, grassroots leaders, civil society organizations, social movements, cultural groups, environmental collectives, and other forms of collective action can play fundamental roles in identifying problems, advocating for rights, mobilizing resources, and developing responses to local needs. By integrating scientific and popular knowledge, these initiatives help to broaden social participation and strengthen the capacity of populations to intervene in the processes that affect their health and living conditions. The role of social movements takes on particular significance in this context, as these collectives can link local demands to broader agendas, such as social justice, equity, environmental protection, and the safeguarding of rights, that remain under-explored in the literature. Identifying experiences within this field can inform the formulation of participatory, socially just, and epidemiologically efficient policies, drawing upon the knowledge and practices rooted in specific territories. Accordingly, this article aims to map studies that examine how social movements have fostered health promotion and contributed to the creation of healthy and sustainable territories globally.

items.title: The Roles of Critical Thinking and Cognitive Load in the Association Between Digital and Perceived Argumentative Writing Readiness Among Indonesian High School Students
items.abstract: Background The increasing emphasis on digital-age competencies in secondary education further supports the notion that students' digital literacy statistically predicts argumentative writing skills. However, it is unclear whether digital literacy directly shapes writing readiness or does so through cognitive mechanisms such as critical thinking and cognitive load, particularly among high school students in Global South countries. Objective This study examines a moderated-mediation model of self-reported argumentative writing readiness, in which critical thinking mediates the relationship between digital literacy and students’ self-reported readiness to write argumentative texts among high school students in Indonesia, while cognitive load is tested as a boundary condition that moderates the strength of the critical thinking to writing readiness relationship. Methods This study applied a cross-sectional survey design with a purposive sample of 513 high school students from 12 districts/cities in South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Data analysis was carried out using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapping, with a significance threshold of 0.05. Results The results showed that digital literacy played a significant role in predicting critical thinking (β = 0.736; p < 0.001), and, in turn, critical thinking significantly predicted argumentative writing readiness (β = 0.656; p < 0.001). The indirect pathway from digital literacy to writing readiness via critical thinking was also significant (β = 0.482; p < 0.001). In contrast, cognitive load did not show a significant relationship with writing readiness (β = − 0.031; p = 0.579), even though it was positively predicted by both digital literacy and critical thinking. Conclusion These findings suggest that critical thinking is the main mechanism that fully mediates the relationship between digital literacy and argumentative writing readiness, and interestingly, this mechanism actually strengthens, not weakens, when the cognitive load is at a higher level. weakens, when the cognitive load is at a higher level. Implicitly, digital skill training alone is not enough to improve students’ writing readiness, unless accompanied by explicit critical thinking instruction. On the other hand, cognitively demanding writing tasks do not always need to be minimized, as long as students have critical thinking skills that let them turn that cognitive engagement into productive reasoning.

items.title: ThinkingGuard: Decoding Implicit Hazards via Step-by-Step Risk Attribution in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, their reliability is threatened by multimodal implicit risks. Unlike explicit threats, these hazards emerge when individually benign text and neutral visual entities logically converge to induce unsafe outputs. Current detection methods fail to address this because they overlook the underlying risk activation mechanisms that govern cross-modal risk activation, leading to single-modality shortcut learning and hallucinated rationalizations. To bridge this gap, we first construct TriggerBench, the first dataset explicitly modeling risk compositionality (5,600 instances). By formally isolating Key Elements and Trigger Elements to build counterfactual contrastive pairs, TriggerBench eliminates risk residues and forces models to perform genuine logical deduction rather than superficial pattern matching, which provides a rigorous foundation for both large-scale training and fine-grained evaluation. Building on this, we propose a Step-Supervised Structured Reasoning training framework and employ it to train ThinkingGuard, a specialized guard model. Inspired by Situation Awareness theory, we decouple implicit risk identification into progressive cognitive stages, and utilize a step-reward Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm to explore optimal reasoning trajectories, which are then distilled into the model through Dual-Constraint Preference Alignment. Extensive experiments across both standard and implicit safety benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkingGuard achieves strong performance. Project resources are available at https://github.com/FroggyChen/ThinkingGuard.

items.title: From Dialogue to Task: How Cognitive Engagement With Generative Artificial Intelligence Relates to Post-Dialogue Activity and Task Outcomes
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded within learning tasks, yet interaction frequency reveals little about cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue. Little is known about how such engagement is situated within task workflows or how dialogue characteristics and subsequent task activity relate to students' behaviour and task outcomes. This study examined cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue, its position within task workflows, and associations of dialogue and task-process characteristics with post-dialogue activity and task outcomes. Data were collected from 1,681 students across 40 university courses using three AI companions embedded in resource creation, peer moderation, and practice. Cognitive engagement in 829 conversation threads was coded with a dialogue-oriented Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, and 2,969 task sequences were modelled with first-order Markov models. Regression models linked dialogue and task-process characteristics to behavioural re-engagement, peer-rated artefact quality, and practice performance. Passive and Active engagement predominated, although resource creation involved more Constructive and Interactive dialogue, peer moderation more Passive, and practice more Active, while higher-engagement dialogue was less often followed by session termination. In resource creation, student-composed messages were associated with more dialogue-to-task returns than template-only requests at the same Passive level, whereas deeper cognitive engagement was associated with higher final artefact quality independent of return frequency; in practice, AI dialogue after an incorrect attempt was associated with fewer further attempts but higher next-attempt correctness among continuers. Post-dialogue activity and task outcomes are distinct aspects of AI use that interaction frequency cannot capture and evaluations should assess separately.

items.title: Just AI Governance and the Forbidden-Boundary Principle
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes consequential decisions, yet predictive accuracy is not a sufficient justification for delegated authority. This conceptual study develops an integrated framework for assessing just AI across normative, data, model, and governance layers. Drawing on plural theories of justice, sociotechnical fairness research, and publicly available governance standards, it maps six justice requirements to observable evidence, decision rights, and remedies. It proposes a two-stage evaluation rule: exclude uses that fail independently justified minimum rights constraints, then compare eligible alternatives across multiple performance and governance criteria. As an explicitly limited normative analogy, Genesis chapter 2 motivates a Forbidden-Boundary Principle (FBP), under which an AI agent must not execute externally consequential actions outside pre-authorized boundaries. The resulting First-Principle Safe-Stop Protocol (FPSSP) comprises an independently governed policy monitor, a mandatory execution gate, a restricted or alternative safe-state controller, immutable-oriented audit trails, and accountable human authorization for recovery. We distinguish this normative and traceability contribution from existing Simplex and runtime assurance architectures; we do not claim a novel safety switch or formal proof of universal ethical compliance. A policy schema, threat model, test matrix, outcome definitions, and a prospective comparison design make the proposal falsifiable. No FPSSP implementation, experimental dataset, numerical improvement, or verified latency bound is reported. The framework supports future evaluation rather than constituting evidence of operational safety.

items.title: Repetition bias in self-directed learning
items.abstract: Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation. People often autonomously organize their own learning into "blocks": they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on. Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice. In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions. We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.
